extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political communication, public opinion, and propaganda
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and techniques for creating, interpreting, and aggregating public opinion: how leaders, symbols, messages, and communication media transfer private interests into a common will and why simple deterministic theories fail to predict opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic determinism (materialistic conception)
rubrics_metrics.description: The materialistic conception of politics ... cannot predict which of a man's many social relations is effecting a particular opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating political theories or seeking to explain public opinion, do not assume economic position uniquely determines a person's views. A single individual has many social relations (landlord, importer, employee, creditor, consumer, etc.), and the materialistic conception cannot tell which relation produces a particular opinion without special inquiry. Use caution in attributing opinions solely to class or economic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive limits of ownership/interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinist can predict in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the owner will resist attempts to deprive him of ownership, or that he will favor legislation which he thinks will increase his profits. But how the function of being an owner will figure, no economic determinist as such, can tell you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broad tendencies (e.g., desire to retain property) as probabilistic rather than determinative of specific policy positions. Do not infer fine-grained policy preferences or time horizons (short vs long view, competitive vs cooperative) from ownership alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class interest is not a fixed set of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no fixed set of opinions on any question that go with being the owner of a factory, no views on labor, on property, on management, let alone views on less immediate matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming a coherent, uniform 'class interest' that supplies a ready-made policy program. The same class may conceive its interests narrowly or broadly, selfishly or unselfishly; evaluators should look for internal diversity and contestation within classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability in conception of class interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A class interest can be conceived largely or narrowly, selfishly or unselfishly, in the light of no facts, some facts, many facts, truth and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists and communicators must account for multiple possible conceptions of interest within any group. Policies or appeals that assume one conception risk failing because members may interpret their interests differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instinctive and hedonistic determinism are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: The socialist theory of human nature is, like the hedonistic calculus, an example of false determinism. Both assume that the unlearned dispositions fatally but intelligently produce a certain type of behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat instincts or pleasure/pain calculus as fixed, standalone predictors of social behavior. Psychological evidence (James, McDougall) suggests instincts are shaped and conditioned by experience; analytical accounts must allow for learning and modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craving and action are learned and historically variable
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no prima facie case then for supposing that because persons crave some particular thing, or behave in some particular way, human nature is fatally constituted to crave that and act thus. The craving and the action are both learned, and in another generation might be learned differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anthropology and psychology indicate the stimuli that excite passions and the means to realize them differ across ages and societies. Explanations and interventions should consider historical and cultural conditioning rather than innate fatalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution and shorthand lead to verbalism (warning about symbolic simplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: He employs a shorthand of names and signs and samples. He has to do this if he is to advance at all... But if he forgets that he has substituted and simplified, he soon lapses into verbalism, and begins to talk about names regardless of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using names/symbols as shorthand for complex realities is necessary, but practitioners must remember the underlying objects. Analysts should be alert to the risk that discourse becomes detached from facts (verbalism) when symbols replace concrete understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioned responses make emotions transferable via symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: By what is known to psychologists as conditioned response, an emotion is not attached merely to one idea... there are no end of things which can arouse the emotion, and no end of things which can satisfy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To build coalitions, identify stimuli (names, images, symbols) that can arouse the same underlying emotion across different groups. Recognize emotion's transferability both as a tool for persuasion and as a factor that can decouple feeling from factual judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'binders' (stereotypes/symbols) to transfer sentiment and unite factions
rubrics_metrics.description: The italicized words are binders: Lincoln in such a speech has of course, no relation to Abraham Lincoln. It is merely a stereotype by which the piety which surrounds that name can be transferred to the Republican candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders can evoke shared sentiments among heterogeneous audiences by invoking respected figures, names, or stereotypes that function as symbolic binders. This is an effective technique for healing schisms and creating a sense of common history or virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness/obscurantism as both technique and symptom
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost always vagueness at a crucial point in public debate is a symptom of cross-purposes. Where superficial harmony is the aim and conflict the fact, obscurantism in a public appeal is the usual result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic ambiguity can unite divergent factions by allowing multiple readings, but it is also a sign that hidden conflicts remain unresolved. Use vagueness deliberately to build broad coalitions, but expect it to mask substantive disagreement and risk future rupture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select non-controversial factual detail to avoid arousing contrary passions
rubrics_metrics.description: On the non-contentious record, the detail is overwhelming; on the issue everything is cloudy. Having got by the two explosive points... the speech passes for a while to safer ground. The candidate tells the story... No contrary passions could be aroused by such a record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When addressing a heterogeneous audience, anchor much of the message in specific, indisputable facts that do not provoke conflicting passions; reserve ambiguity for divisive issues while using concrete detail to build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic ambiguity: craft statements readable differently by factions
rubrics_metrics.description: The theme 'friendship' is for the non-interventionists, the theme 'new policy' and 'firmness' is for the interventionists... The formula covers two diametrically opposed purposes by the symbolic phrase 'American rights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose key phrases or themes that can be interpreted to satisfy different constituencies simultaneously (strategic ambiguity). This enables broad appeal but requires skill to avoid obvious contradiction that would alienate base groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols as strategic convergence points (control over symbols implies control over public approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: They are like a strategic railroad center where many roads converge regardless of their ultimate origin or their ultimate destination. But he who captures the symbols by which public feeling is for the moment contained, controls by that much the approaches of public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize symbols (e.g., 'Americanism', 'Lincoln') as contested strategic assets. Political actors should strive to possess and define dominant symbols, because control of symbolic language shapes the possibilities for policy and coalition-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of symbolic power: overuse or abuse can 'burst' a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Too violent abuse of the actualities which groups of people think the symbol represents, or too great resistance in the name of that symbol to new purposes, will, so to speak, burst the symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that symbols have resilience limits: excessive mismatch between symbol and reality or rigid resistance to change can destroy the symbol's power. Monitor symbolic credibility and avoid actions that would rupture shared meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use modern communication technologies to knit common consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: It was an attempt to exploit the modern machinery of communication to start a return to a 'common consciousness' throughout the world. Without cable, telegraph, and daily press, radio, the experiment of the Fourteen Points would have been impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synchronous, wide-reaching media and communication infrastructures (press, telegraph, radio) enable leaders to address large populations with shared names and ideas simultaneously; leverage media to distribute unifying symbols and narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting aggregates do not reveal underlying motives
rubrics_metrics.description: By counting the votes on election day you do not know the real division of opinion about the League. There were, for example, nine million Democrats. Are you entitled to believe that all of them are staunch supporters of the League? Certainly you are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer detailed public opinion or policy commitments from aggregate electoral outcomes. Votes compress many motives into binary choices; analysts should investigate context and cross-pressures rather than assuming uniformity among voters of the same ticket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political change can arise from a shared least common denominator
rubrics_metrics.description: For the least common denominator of all the votes was that the Democrats should go and the Republicans come in. That was the only factor remaining after all the contradictions had cancelled each other out. But that factor was enough to alter policy for four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many conflicting motives cancel each other, a simple, shallow shared desire (least common denominator) can produce decisive political outcomes. Strategists can exploit this by focusing appeals on a minimal, widely-shared objective to secure change.
